title: Beringia first flooded, linking Arctic and Pacific

facts.text: The land bridge between Alaska and Siberia was first flooded near the start of the Pliocene, letting marine life spread between the Arctic and Pacific.
The bridge was flooded and restored again and again afterwards.
The Bering Strait is thought to have first opened between 7.4 and 4.8 million years ago.

conflicts.note: Bering Strait page: opening of the strait

facts.text: The first tree sloths appeared around the start of the Pliocene.
Early megalonychid sloths were small and perhaps partly tree-dwelling; by the Pliocene they reached about half the size of later Megalonyx.
Living tree sloths are thought to have evolved from ground sloth ancestors, which makes ground sloths a paraphyletic group.
During the Pliocene and Pleistocene, as part of the Great American Interchange, additional sloth lineages migrated into Central and North America.

conflicts.note: Timeline of life: rounded

facts.text: The nimravids, cat-like carnivores, died out around the start of the Pliocene.
Nimravids had still been diverse in the Early Miocene.

conflicts.note: Timeline of life: rounded

title: Zanclean flood refills the Mediterranean

facts.text: Atlantic water broke through at the Strait of Gibraltar and refilled the dried-out Mediterranean, ending the Messinian salinity crisis.
About ninety percent of the basin may have filled within months to two years, with sea level at times rising over 10 metres a day.
Peak discharge is estimated at about 100 million cubic metres per second, roughly a thousand times today's Amazon.
Seawater flooded the deep canyon cut by the ancestral Nile up to at least Aswan; the modern Nile then began filling it with sediment.
The reconnection marks the start of the Zanclean age, the first age of the Pliocene.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether the Mediterranean refilled in one catastrophic flood or more gradually, and its exact timing is uncertain.

title: Oreodonts disappear

facts.text: Oreodonts, plant-eating hoofed mammals that had stayed diverse since the Oligocene, disappeared in the earliest Pliocene.

title: Pliocene marine megafauna extinction

facts.text: A marine megafauna extinction in the Pliocene wiped out 36% of large marine species, including 55% of marine mammals, 35% of seabirds, 9% of sharks and 43% of sea turtles.
It struck warm-blooded and partly warm-blooded animals harder than cold-blooded ones, pointing to a shrinking food supply.
Plio-Pleistocene sea-level swings, the largest of the Cenozoic and driven by growing polar ice, damaged coastal habitats and may have helped cause several marine megafauna extinctions.
After the Central American Seaway closed, tropical whales declined in diversity and abundance.

title: Sierra Nevada uplifted and tilted westward

facts.text: Between two and three million years ago, during the Pliocene, the Sierra Nevada was uplifted and tilted westward.
The range began rising less than five million years ago, and faulting still lifts it, building steep escarpments on its eastern edge.
Its age is argued: some read recent river incision as young uplift, others find the northern range little changed since 30-40 million years ago.

title: Mount Kenya volcano builds up

facts.text: Mount Kenya, a large stratovolcano on the shoulder of the East African Rift, was active in the Plio-Pleistocene.
Its original summit was probably over 6,000 m high, perhaps 7,000 m, taller than Kilimanjaro is today.
Since it went extinct, glaciers have eroded it; its remains are Africa's second-highest mountain, topped by Batian at 5,199 m.

title: Colorado River begins cutting the Grand Canyon

facts.text: When the Gulf of California opened 5.3 million years ago it lowered the Colorado River's base level, speeding the erosion that cut most of the canyon's depth by 1.2 Ma.
Several recent studies hold that the river set its course through the area 5-6 million years ago; the Marble Canyon and westernmost segments were carved since then.
The canyon's age is debated: other studies put parts at 17 to 70 million years old, and consensus holds that segments formed at different times and later joined.

contested_note: The age of the Grand Canyon is debated between 'young river' (5-6 Ma) and 'old river' (up to 70 Ma) views.

facts.text: The great white shark evolved about 5.3 million years ago.
Abundant juvenile teeth show that Pliocene coasts of Chile's Coquimbo Region served as great white shark nurseries.
From about 5.3 to 2.7 Ma a warm interval, the Pliocene Warm Interval, interrupted the long-term cooling trend.
The Pliocene opened with warmer global temperatures than the cooler Messinian before it.
Carbon dioxide levels were similar to today's, so the interval is often treated as an analogue for near-future warming.
Ice-sheet collapses were much more common in the early to mid Pliocene, between 5 and 3 Ma.
The oceans stayed relatively warm, though they kept cooling.
Fossils at Bluff Downs in northern Queensland were laid down about 5.2-3.6 million years ago, beside large water bodies fringed by riverside forests.
It is one of Australia's most significant Pliocene sites, with marsupials from both living and extinct families.
The fossil beds are at least 4 million years old and lie beneath a basalt flow dated 3.62 Ma.

verification.title: New potassium‐argon basalt date in relation to the Pliocene Bluff Downs Local Fauna, northern Australia

title: Kauaʻi forms over the Hawaiian hotspot

facts.text: Kauaʻi, the oldest of the main Hawaiian islands, formed as the Pacific Plate passed over the Hawaiʻi hotspot.
Potassium-argon dating gives Kauaʻi an age of 5.1 ± 0.2 million years, little more than 5 million years.
The chain's volcanoes get younger to the southeast, as the plate carries each one west-northwest away from the hotspot.

sources.title: List of volcanoes in the Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain

title: Colorado Plateau and River take modern shape

facts.text: About 5 million years ago the Colorado Plateau reached its present height and the Colorado River took a course close to today's.
Plateau uplift and the opening of the Gulf of California by 5 Ma rearranged the drainage of the Colorado and its tributaries.
About 4 million years ago the Colorado River began reaching the Salton Trough, still connected then to the Gulf of California.

sources.title: Geology of the Bryce Canyon area

facts.text: Teeth from Australia and South Africa show that Livyatan or a close relative still hunted around 5 million years ago, possibly worldwide.
These giant-toothed sperm whales died out by the early Pliocene.
Cooling probably made baleen whales larger and fewer, and the raptorial whales that fed on them declined with them.
Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion, first appeared in the Pliocene; its early species T. crassidentatus, about 5 million years ago, was the size of a large dog.
Its later species grew to lioness weight and the genus became Australia's apex predator, the only one of its family until the end of the Pleistocene.

conflicts.note: Thylacoleo lead and infobox give a Late Pliocene start (3.6-2.58 Ma)

facts.text: From about 5 million years ago the Paratethys Sea grew steadily shallower and largely dried out.
During the Pliocene it split into a few inland seas that were at times fully cut off from each other.
The Black, Caspian and Aral seas are its remnants; the Pliocene Caspian was a small lake without an outlet.

title: Pliocene ignimbrite pulse in the northern Puna

facts.text: Between 5 and 3.8 Ma, large-scale ignimbrite eruptions struck the arc front of the northern Puna, part of a magma pulse around 4 Ma.
The Puripicar ignimbrite of about 4.2 Ma alone held some 1,500 cubic kilometres.
Later giants include the 3.49-million-year-old Tara ignimbrite (800 km3) and the 2.89-million-year-old Pastos Grandes ignimbrite (1,500 km3).
Between 4.9 and 4.5 million years ago a sinkhole pond in a warm, wet forest in Tennessee trapped plants and animals.
It is the first site of its age known from Appalachia, yielding new species of red panda, rhinoceros, pond turtle and hickory.
Its fossils show eastern North America still shared a biogeographic link with Eurasia in the Early Pliocene.
The Kilgore Tuff eruption in eastern Idaho, rated VEI 8, blasted out about 1,800 cubic kilometres of ash and left a caldera 80 by 60 km.
It was the last caldera-forming eruption of the Heise volcanic field, active for over 2 million years above the Yellowstone hotspot.
Between 5 and 3.3 Ma, the Picabo and Heise centres subsided as the hotspot track moved northeast.

facts.text: The early hominin Ardipithecus ramidus lived in the Afar region of Ethiopia about 4.4 million years ago.
Its most complete specimen is 'Ardi', a 4.4-million-year-old female skeleton.
Ardi's pelvis shows bipedal walking was well under way by then, though her hands and limbs could still climb trees.
Fossils of at least nine more individuals from As Duma in the Afar date to 4.51-4.32 million years ago.
The older A. kadabba is considered its direct ancestor.

conflicts.note: As Duma (Gona) fossils

facts.text: Australopithecus anamensis, the oldest known Australopithecus species, lived roughly 4.3 to 3.8 million years ago.
Its first fossils came from Kanapoi and Allia Bay in northern Kenya; the Allia Bay finds give the earliest evidence of a bipedal gait.
Australopithecus probably arose in eastern Africa around 4 Ma, later spread across the continent, and died out somewhat after 2 Ma.
A nearly complete 3.8-million-year-old skull from Ethiopia shows it overlapped in time with A. afarensis.

title: Atana ignimbrite supereruption at La Pacana

facts.text: La Pacana caldera in the Chilean Andes erupted the giant Atana ignimbrite between about 4.2 and 3.8 million years ago.
At 2,500-3,500 cubic kilometres, it is the fifth-largest explosive eruption known.
The much smaller Toconao ignimbrite erupted at almost the same time, with no sign of a pause between the two.

facts.text: The Hagerman fossil beds in Idaho date from at least 4 million to 3.07 million years ago and hold at least 200 species.
They are among the richest Blancan deposits and hold the largest known concentration of the Hagerman horse, Equus simplicidens.

conflicts.note: List of lagerstätten
Evolution of the horse: single point

facts.text: The giant armoured glyptodonts Glyptodon and Glyptotherium evolved in South America from about 3.9 million years ago.
Glyptodon, a herbivorous armadillo relative with a shell of hundreds of bony plates, reached 2 m long and 400 kg.
Glyptodon itself is known from about 3.2 million years ago until the early Holocene, about 11,000 years ago.

conflicts.note: Glyptodon lead: first appearance of the genus itself

facts.text: Australopithecus afarensis lived in East Africa from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago.
The 3.58-million-year-old Kadanuumuu skeleton suggests the species already walked fully upright by 3.6 Ma, though not all researchers agree.
Selam, a three-year-old girl from Dikika, Ethiopia, dates to 3.3 Ma, about 100,000 years before Lucy.
Tooth chemistry shows a flexible diet, from forest plants to open savanna plants.
Africa then held more large carnivores than today, including hyenas and saber-toothed cats, which likely preyed on australopithecines.

title: Extended humid period in North Africa

facts.text: North Africa went through an extended humid period from about 3.8 to 3.3 million years ago.
Tropical forests in northwestern Africa reached as far as Cape Blanc until around 3.5 Ma.
A significant Saharan river flowed until 3.35 Ma, when trade winds began to dominate.

title: Earliest woolly rhinoceros lineage in Tibet

facts.text: Coelodonta thibetana, the oldest known species of the woolly rhinoceros genus, lived in Tibet about 3.7 million years ago.
The genus had spread to Siberia, Mongolia and China by the Early Pleistocene; the woolly rhinoceros itself appeared later, in the Middle Pleistocene.
At Laetoli in Tanzania, early hominins, probably Australopithecus, left footprints in fresh volcanic ash about 3.7 million years ago.
Soft rain then cemented the powdery ash into tuff, preserving the prints.
The tracks were made by three individuals, one walking in the footprints of another.
With the leg bones, the trackways suggest A. afarensis was a competent biped, though less efficient at walking than humans.
Dated to 3.7 million years ago within the upper Laetolil Beds (3.8-3.6 Ma), the prints were then the oldest known evidence of hominin bipedalism and closely resemble modern human footprints.

verification.title: Laetoli Footprints Preserve Earliest Direct Evidence of Human-Like Bipedal Biomechanics
verification.note: The paper's 3.6 Ma for the same footprints lies within the event's 3.8–3.6 Ma bracket; this is a rounding difference.

title: Little Foot skeleton at Sterkfontein

facts.text: Little Foot, an Australopithecus skeleton from the Sterkfontein caves of South Africa, is about 90% complete, the most complete early hominin skeleton known.
A 2015 radioisotopic date of 3.67 million years makes it the earliest known South African australopith, contemporary with A. afarensis.
Its dating is controversial, with estimates from 2.2 to 3.67 million years, and whether it belongs to A. africanus or another species is disputed.

contested_note: The age of Little Foot (2.2 to 3.67 Ma) and its species are disputed.

conflicts.note: 2014 estimate

Full range of published estimates

facts.text: The oldest remains of Megatherium, the giant ground sloth of South America, come from Bolivia and the Pampas and are at least 3.6 million years old.
The genus lasted to the end of the Late Pleistocene; its best-known species, M. americanum, was elephant-sized at 3.5-4 tonnes.
About 3.6 million years ago an impact on the Chukchi Peninsula of northeast Siberia blasted out a crater 18 km across.
The crater now holds a lake about 12 km wide whose sediments record Arctic climate, such as summers 8 °C warmer in the mid-Pliocene.
Megalodon, a giant shark estimated at 14-24 m long and among the most powerful predators ever, hunted worldwide from about 23 million years ago.
A 2019 statistical reanalysis of its fossil record moved its extinction back to about 3.6 million years ago, earlier than the long-assumed 2.6 million years.
Cooling seas, falling sea levels that shrank its warm nursery waters, and the decline of small baleen whales probably combined to finish it.
Competition from early killer whales, once blamed, now looks unlikely; rivalry with white sharks may have played a part instead.
Its loss let great white sharks spread into waters it had held, and baleen whales grew markedly larger afterwards.

facts.text: The elephant genera Elephas and Mammuthus (mammoths) migrated out of Africa in the late Pliocene, around 3.6 to 3.2 million years ago.
Elephants, gomphotheres and stegodonts thrived in Asia, though proboscidean diversity fell sharply during the Late Pliocene.
By 3.2 million years ago mammoths had dispersed into Eurasia via the Sinai Peninsula, entering Europe around 3 million years ago.
In Africa, mammoths became confined to the north of the continent by the Late Pliocene.

facts.text: Jaw fossils from Koro Toro in Chad, about 3.5 million years old, are the first and only australopiths known from Central Africa.
They show australopiths ranged widely across Africa, not just in the east and south; many researchers still assign them to A. afarensis.
They lived in lakeside grassland with sparse trees by an expanded 'Lake Mega-Chad', apparently eating mostly savanna foods.

conflicts.note: 2008 10Be/9Be date of the enclosing sediment
2010 redating

facts.text: Kenyanthropus, a flat-faced, small-toothed hominin, lived by Lake Turkana in Kenya; its type skull, lying between tuffs of 3.57 and 3.4 Ma, is about 3.5 million years old.
Its fossils span about 3.5 to 3.2 Ma and show that more than one hominin lineage lived in the Middle Pliocene alongside A. afarensis.
It shared a lakeside or floodplain mix of forest and grassland, and may have made the Lomekwian stone tools found at the same site.

conflicts.note: Kenyanthropus lead dates the Lomekwi finds

title: Camels live in the High Arctic

facts.text: Fragmentary camel remains, referred to Paracamelus, come from Ellesmere Island inside the Arctic Circle and are about 3.4 million years old.
Global temperatures were then 2-3 °C warmer than today, and the island was covered in boreal forest.
Collagen sequences confirm these High Arctic camels were close relatives of modern Camelus.

title: Disputed cut-marked bones at Dikika

facts.text: At Dikika, Ethiopia, a rib from a cow-sized hoofed animal and a juvenile bovid femur bear cut marks, the rib also some crushing.
If made by stone tools, they would be the oldest evidence of butchering with sharp-edged tools, at 3.4 million years, attributable to Australopithecus afarensis.
The claim is disputed: the bones lay in sandstone, where abrasive sand and gravel also scratched them.

contested_note: Whether hominins made the marks is disputed; abrasion in sandstone makes the attribution weak.

verification.title: Evidence for stone-tool-assisted consumption of animal tissues before 3.39 million years ago at Dikika, Ethiopia

facts.text: The oldest known stone tools, from Lomekwi 3 in West Turkana, Kenya, date to 3.3 million years ago.
Their makers are unknown; Kenyanthropus platyops, a 3.5-3.2-million-year-old hominin from Lake Turkana, may have been the earliest tool user.
Cut-marked animal bones about 3.4 million years old from Ethiopia's Lower Awash Valley may be even older, indirect evidence of tool use.
The Paleolithic, which covers almost all of humanity's prehistoric technology, begins with the first stone tools about 3.3 million years ago.
The Lomekwian tools are simple flakes struck by pounding a core on an anvil or with a hammerstone, made from volcanic rock gathered within 100 m.

facts.text: About 3.3 million years ago spreading on the Antarctic-Phoenix Ridge stopped, and subduction of the Phoenix plate slowed or ceased after over 100 million years.
The plate's remnant was absorbed into the Antarctic plate.

title: Possible impact in Argentina

facts.text: A possible cosmic impact struck Argentina about 3.3 million years ago, at the start of the Marplatan land-mammal age.
It has been suggested as a cause of the turnover of South American fauna, but this remains controversial.

contested_note: Both the impact and its link to the South American faunal turnover are uncertain; the sources call the link controversial.

verification.title: A 3.3-Ma Impact in Argentina and Possible Consequences

facts.text: Between 3.3 and 3.0 million years ago, global temperatures were 2-3 °C above today's, with carbon dioxide near 400 ppm, like the year 2000.
This peak of Pliocene warmth is also called the Pliocene Thermal Maximum.
Arctic summers were about 8 °C warmer than today, and Greenland's ice was limited to its highest eastern and southern peaks.
In southeastern European lakes, viviparid snails diversified rapidly as temperatures rose by as much as 10 °C between 3.3 and 2.9 Ma.
Global sea level stood about 25 m higher than today, and models suggest the Arctic above 70°N was 10-20 °C warmer, with little change in the tropics.
Australopithecus africanus lived in South Africa from about 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago; its fossils come from Taung, Sterkfontein, Makapansgat and Gladysvale.
Its first specimen, the Taung Child, a juvenile skull about 2.8 million years old, was the first early hominin ever found.
A competent biped, though less efficient than humans, it kept a more apelike upper body than East Africa's A. afarensis.
It lived in gallery forest bordered by grassland and ate a highly varied diet, including C4 foods such as grasses and seeds.
It probably died out because of strong climatic volatility and perhaps competition with Homo and Paranthropus robustus.

conflicts.note: Earlier dating of Sterkfontein Member 4 specimens

facts.text: Lucy, a female Australopithecus afarensis whose skeleton is about 40% complete, lived at Hadar in Ethiopia's Afar region around 3.2 million years ago.
Ash layers beneath the fossil were argon-dated to 3.22 and 3.18 Ma; the younger lies only one metre below her.
Her small, ape-like skull paired with an upright, bipedal gait shows that walking upright came before larger brains.
Nearby, the 'First Family' site AL 333, about 3.2 million years old, holds at least thirteen individuals of different ages.

title: Permanent El Niño ends in the eastern Pacific

facts.text: A permanent El Niño-like state kept the eastern equatorial Pacific warm in the early to mid Pliocene, lowering Earth's reflectivity.
Around 3 million years ago cold surface water appeared there, which may have aided global cooling and changed climate's response to orbital cycles.

verification.title: Role of tropics in changing the response to Milankovich forcing some three million years ago

facts.text: Around 3 million years ago savanna expanded in East Africa as the climate turned cooler and drier.
Pliocene global cooling may have hastened the disappearance of forests and the spread of grasslands and savannas.
One hypothesis holds that walking upright and other hominin traits evolved as Pliocene climate change turned forests into more open savannah.
Moving from dense forest to savanna, where wildfires were common but easier to survive, may have been the first step toward early humans' control of fire.

sources.title: Control of fire by early humans

verification.title: The pyrophilic primate hypothesis
verification.venue: Evolutionary Anthropology Issues News and Reviews

facts.text: Roughly 3 million years ago South America's native carnivore guild collapsed, including the last sparassodonts, the continent's meat-eating metatherians.
Thylacosmilids last occur about 3 Ma, already rarer before the interchange; terror birds also declined after that.
The collapse did not match the arrival of carnivorans: dogs and weasels reached South America about 2.9 Ma but stayed rare until the Pleistocene.
By the Pliocene only two sparassodont families were left; hathliacynids are last known from the early Pliocene.
The long sparassodont decline from the Late Miocene to the end of the Pliocene may be linked to cooling and the onset of Quaternary glaciation.
The South Asian Summer Monsoon grew stronger after 2.95 Ma, probably because the Indonesian Throughflow was reorganized.
The Oldowan (Mode I), the first widespread stone-tool industry, was used by hominins across much of Africa from about 2.9 Ma until at least 1.7 Ma.
The oldest known Oldowan tools come from Nyayanga on the Homa Peninsula in Kenya, dated to about 2.9 million years ago.
Thousands of artifacts at Gona, Ethiopia, are firmly dated to 2.6 Ma by radioisotopes and magnetostratigraphy.
Sharp-edged tools of about 2.6 Ma at Ledi-Geraru may be the work of early Homo; Australopithecus garhi is another candidate maker.
The tools served mainly for butchering: 2.5-million-year-old tools lay beside cut-marked bones, and Homo habilis made Oldowan tools from about 2.3 Ma.

title: Isthmus of Panama joins the Americas

facts.text: South America became attached to North America through the newly formed Isthmus of Panama around 2.8 million years ago.
Raised at a convergent plate margin, partly by volcanism, it closed the last strait outside the polar regions linking the Pacific and Atlantic.
Surface-water exchange through the seaway may already have been fading by 4.6-4.2 Ma; the closing cut Pacific nutrients off from the Caribbean 4.5-3 Ma.
Closure ended the last remnant of a circum-equatorial current that had flowed since the Cretaceous, and pushed more heat and salt toward the North Atlantic.
Strengthened Gulf Stream and Humboldt currents cooled the Arctic, eventually leading to the Quaternary ice age glaciations.

facts.text: The oldest known fossil of the genus Homo, the jawbone LD 350-1 from Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia's Afar region, dates to 2.8-2.75 million years ago.
Its age suggests Homo may have evolved from Australopithecus afarensis around this time.
Homo is assumed to have emerged by about 2.8 Ma, most likely from australopithecine ancestors in East Africa's Rift Valley.
Teeth from Koobi Fora, Kenya, dated 3-2.7 Ma, may belong to the same species.
The origin of Homo 2.8-2.5 Ma coincided with climatic changes, but too few fossils are known to tell whether climate was the cause.

facts.text: From around 2.7 million years ago the new land bridge set off the last and largest wave of migration between the Americas.
Cats, condors, raccoons and camelids moved south; armadillos, hummingbirds and opossums moved north.
Ground sloths and glyptodonts reached North America; xenarthrans were among South America's most successful emigrants.
Horses and tapirs entered South America, where competition from northern hoofed mammals helped push native ungulates toward extinction.
The exchange was lopsided: extinction rates were much higher in South America, and North American groups diversified greatly there.

facts.text: Around 2.7 million years ago temperatures dropped and glaciation began in the Northern Hemisphere.
Greenland's separate ice caps merged into one ice sheet covering most of the island once carbon dioxide fell to 280-320 ppm, 2.7-2.6 Ma.
Ice-rafted cobbles on North Atlantic and North Pacific seabeds and an abrupt shift in oxygen isotopes mark the new Arctic ice.
Suggested causes include falling carbon dioxide and a stronger North Atlantic circulation after Panama closed, which carried moisture north.
A weakening Indonesian Throughflow cut heat transport toward Antarctica, cooling Earth in a self-reinforcing loop as sea levels fell.

facts.text: The robust hominin genus Paranthropus evolved around 2.7 million years ago.
Paranthropus aethiopicus is known from Lake Turkana, Kenya, and the genus was still present at the start of the Pleistocene.
Its earliest species, P. aethiopicus, lived in East Africa about 2.7-2.3 Ma; the oldest remains, from Ethiopia's Omo Kibish Formation, date to 2.6 Ma.

title: Nearby supernovae leave iron-60 on the seafloor

facts.text: Radioactive iron-60, which only supernovae can make, points to a large influx about 2.6 million years ago, recorded in ancient seabed deposits.
A scattered excess over 10 million years suggests several relatively close supernovae, perhaps from the passing Scorpius-Centaurus OB association.
So close an explosion could have damaged Earth's ozone layer and killed some ocean life.
